name: Lighters, matches and ferro rods
summary: Anything that makes a flame or a hot spark on demand: disposable and refillable butane lighters, Zippo-type fluid lighters, matches and ferrocerium rods.
uses: Lighting stoves, lamps, candles and fires; each light used up is one fewer for later, so light the next one from a stove's coals or a standing pilot rather than striking again (but put lamps and candles out before you sleep)
Disposable and refillable gas lighters: the easiest flame, but weak or dead below freezing (MSR fuels): carry one in an inside pocket
Zippo-type fluid lighters: refuel, re-flint and re-wick with spares, so one lasts for years (Zippo fill, Zippo flint, Zippo wick)

Strike-anywhere matches ignite by friction on any solid surface, so keep them in a closed box apart from other things (US rules pack them that way, 49 CFR 173.186). Safety matches ignite only on a prepared surface like the box's striker, so keep the striker (RSC matches)
A spent gas lighter's flint wheel still throws sparks onto very fine tinder: see the fire starting guide
identify: Gas lighters burn liquefied n-butane or isobutane; Canada requires child resistance on every lighter except luxury ones (refillable, over $2.50, not utility), and caps a basic gas lighter's flame at 50 mm (2 in) (Lighters Regulations). Disposables have no fill valve. Refillable gas lighters have a small fill valve on the bottom and usually a flame adjuster; torch lighters give a hard blue jet from a push-button piezo. Utility (long-reach, BBQ) lighters are 100 mm (4 in) or longer (Lighters Regulations). Wick lighters (Zippo type) burn a low-pressure liquid hydrocarbon such as hexane, soaked into packing, with a wick and a flint under a spring screw (Lighters Regulations, Zippo fill, Zippo flint). Strike-anywhere match heads hold tetraphosphorus trisulfide (P4S3) and potassium chlorate and ignite by friction on any solid surface; safety matches keep the red phosphorus on the box's striker and ignite only on a prepared surface (RSC matches, 49 CFR 173.186). A ferro rod is ferrocerium, a rare-earth alloy; a hard steel striker with a sharp edge shaves off particles that burn as hot sparks (Wikipedia ferrocerium).
test: Gas lighter: look at the fuel level through a clear body, then try it. A spark with no flame means empty, too cold or air in the tank; warm it in your hand or an inside pocket and try again, since n-butane boils at about -1 °C (30 °F) and isobutane at about -12 °C (11 °F), and a cold one has little pressure (MSR fuels). A wheel that turns with no spark has a worn flint (Zippo not lighting). Hissing or a gas smell when it is off means a leaking valve: keep it away from flame and pockets. Zippo type: a wheel that spins without sparking needs a new flint; a wick that won't feed fuel needs pulling up and trimming, and after two or three trims it needs replacing (Zippo not lighting, Zippo wick); an empty lighter needs fuel (Zippo not lighting). Matches: strike one from each box. Ferro rod: scrape it hard with the back of a knife or the striker: you should get a shower of sparks.

decay.note: Estimate, with no maker figure found: gas lighters can lose fuel over the years, fluid lighters dry out when unused, and matches keep if dry. Demand, not decay, empties the shelves.

improvise: Refilling a gas lighter: use only the fuel its instructions name (Lighters Regulations). Do it outdoors or somewhere well ventilated with no open flame near, so not beside a lit stove, lamp or candle (Zippo butane). Zippo's method for its butane inserts is upside down with the valve aimed away from your face, 5–6 seconds of fuel, a quick press of the valve to release trapped air, 5–6 seconds more, then at least 2 minutes before lighting (Zippo butane). Escaping butane is very cold and extremely flammable (Zippo butane). Disposable lighters have no valve and aren't made to be refilled; drilling or forcing one is a burn and frostbite risk, so use the gas in it and keep the flint wheel. Zippo type: lighter fluid only, filled slowly into the packing, not overfilled, and the lighter and your hands dried before lighting (Zippo fill). It is flammable fluid: close the can and check nothing has spilled before you light, and don't put a lighter with fuel on its outside into a pocket or next to skin (Zippo fill). Spare flints and wicks are tiny: take them with the lighter. Without any lighter or match: a grill or heater piezo clicker, steel wool on a 9 V battery, magnesium shavings or a lens; see the fire starting guide. Save every light: light a lamp or candle from the stove or a standing pilot instead of striking a new match, and put lamps and candles out before you sleep. Bank coals only in a stove or fireplace vented to the outside and leave its damper open until the ashes are cold, with a working CO alarm: the CPSC warns of poisonous gas building up while people sleep if the damper is closed on warm ashes (CPSC fireplaces).
